To access Reserved Tier, contact your AWS account team.\\n* Request for quota increase by contacting your account manager or AWS Support if your workload traffic exceeds your account quotas\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/troubleshooting-api-error-codes.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"How do I troubleshoot the \\\"ThrottlingException\\\" error when I use Amazon Bedrock on-demand resources?\",\"context\":\"### Monitor your AWS service quotas\\n\\nReview your [Amazon Bedrock service quotas](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/quotas.html) to make sure that you didn't exceed them. Check Amazon CloudWatch metrics at 1-minute increments to identify throttling patterns. When your usage exceeds the quotas at peak times, resource throttle can occur even with previously successful batches. To make sure that your application's request volume doesn't exceed the quotas, monitor the\u00a0**InputTokenCount** and **Invocations** [Amazon Bedrock runtime metrics](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/monitoring-runtime-metrics.html).\\n\\nSpecific models have separate quotas for Requests Per Minute (RPM) and Tokens Per Minute (TPM) that Amazon Bedrock enforces concurrently.\\n\\nNewer model versions can have different quotas than previous versions.\\n\\n**Note:** The Service Quota dashboard shows only configured quotas, not real-time usage. Resubmit\\nyour request later or in a different region. You can also purchase Provisioned\\nThroughput (<https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prov-throughput.html>)\\nto increase the rate or number of tokens you can process\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sdk-for-go/api/service/bedrockruntime/index.html\"},{\"rank_order\":4,\"title\":\"Quotas for the bedrock-mantle endpoint\",\"context\":\"## How requests are evaluated against quotas\\n\\nWhen you submit an inference request to the `bedrock-mantle` endpoint, AWS evaluates it against your quotas in the following order:\\n\\n1. **Input tokens per minute** \u2013 The number of input tokens in the request, plus the value of `max_tokens` (or the model-specific maximum if `max_tokens` is not set), is checked against the input-tokens-per-minute quota for the requested model. If admitting the request would exceed the quota, the request is throttled with an HTTP 429 response.\\n2. **Output tokens per minute** \u2013 As the model streams or generates output, output tokens are counted against the output-tokens-per-minute quota for that model. If the quota is reached during generation, generation stops and the response is returned with a finish reason indicating the cutoff.\\n\\nAfter the response completes, any unused portion of the initial input-token reservation (the difference between `max_tokens` and the actual output) is replenished to your quota.\\n\\nThe endpoint may apply additional internal rate limiting that is not exposed in Service Quotas. Use retry logic with exponential backoff to handle transient throttling.\\n\\nThe `bedrock-runtime` endpoint's TPM quotas count input and output tokens together against a single per-model quota, while the `bedrock-mantle` endpoint applies separate input-tokens-per-minute and output-tokens-per-minute quotas. If you run workloads on both endpoints, plan capacity for each endpoint independently. For details on the runtime endpoint's quotas, see Quotas for the bedrock-runtime endpoint\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/quotas-mantle.html\"},{\"rank_order\":5,\"title\":\"Scaling and throughput best practices\",\"context\":\"## `bedrock-runtime` endpoint: throughput and quotas\\n\\nThe `bedrock-runtime` endpoint has the following quota behavior:\\n\\n* Per-model, per-Region token quotas count input and output tokens together. Output tokens consume quota according to a model-specific burndown rate.\\n* Some models also have RPM quotas, while other models are governed only by token quotas. Check the quotas that apply to the exact model and inference profile that you use.\\n* Per-minute and per-day token quotas are shared across the inference APIs that call the same model on this endpoint. Allocations for `bedrock-runtime` and `bedrock-mantle` are independent.\\n* Custom inference profiles, batch inference, and Provisioned Throughput have separate quotas and are available only through `bedrock-runtime`.\\n\\nFor current quota values, token-burndown details, and the quota-increase process, see Quotas for the bedrock-runtime endpoint. {"id": "f77ad065-27c6-45f6-9188-5ff0694d4e80", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Start with a quota increase, plus a few cheap fixes. Move to provisioned throughput (or Reserved Tier, if your model supports it) only if the demand is steady and predictable.

**When each option fits**

| Option | Fits when | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|
| **Quota increase** | Peaks are occasional or bursty, and you're still on on-demand. | It's a request to AWS Support or your account team, so approval and timing aren't guaranteed. You still pay per token. |
| **Provisioned throughput** | Load is sustained and predictable, and you need guaranteed capacity. | You pay for the capacity whether or not you use it. Availability varies by model and Region. It's only available on `bedrock-runtime`. Cross-Region inference profiles don't support it. |

The docs recommend Reserved Tier or Provisioned Throughput for predictable, sustained throughput. They recommend a quota increase when your traffic exceeds your account quotas. If you only hit limits during peak hours, a commitment will probably sit idle the rest of the day.

**Things to try first or alongside**
1. **Cross-Region inference profiles (geographic or global).** They spread bursts across Regions and often raise effective throughput. Quotas for global profiles are managed in your source Region through Service Quotas.
2. **Lower `max_tokens`.** On `bedrock-runtime`, TPM counts input and output tokens together, and output tokens are weighted by a model-specific burndown rate. An oversized `max_tokens` reserves quota you never use, so right-sizing it can cut throttling a lot.
3. **Retries with exponential backoff and jitter.** AWS recommends this for 429s.
4. **Batch inference for non-urgent work.** It has separate quotas, so it moves load off the on-demand path.

**How to decide**
- Check the CloudWatch `InputTokenCount` and `Invocations` metrics at 1-minute granularity, plus the throttle count. The Service Quotas dashboard only shows configured limits, not live usage.
- If peak usage is roughly 1.5–2x your current TPM and only lasts a short time each day, request an increase and use cross-Region inference.

**When each option fits**

| Option | Fits when | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|
| **Quota increase** | Peaks are occasional or bursty, and you're still on on-demand. | It's a request to AWS Support or your account team, so approval and timing aren't guaranteed. You still pay per token. |
| **Provisioned throughput** | Load is sustained and predictable, and you need guaranteed capacity. | You pay for the capacity whether or not you use it. Availability varies by model and Region. It's only available on `bedrock-runtime`. Cross-Region inference profiles don't support it. |

The docs recommend Reserved Tier or Provisioned Throughput for predictable, sustained throughput. They recommend a quota increase when your traffic exceeds your account quotas. If you only hit limits during peak hours, a commitment will probably sit idle the rest of the day.

**Things to try first or alongside**
1. **Cross-Region inference profiles (geographic or global).** They spread bursts across Regions and often raise effective throughput. Quotas for global profiles are managed in your source Region through Service Quotas.
2. **Lower `max_tokens`.** On `bedrock-runtime`, TPM counts input and output tokens together, and output tokens are weighted by a model-specific burndown rate. An oversized `max_tokens` reserves quota you never use, so right-sizing it can cut throttling a lot.
3. **Retries with exponential backoff and jitter.** AWS recommends this for 429s.
4. **Batch inference for non-urgent work.** It has separate quotas, so it moves load off the on-demand path.

**How to decide**
- Check the CloudWatch `InputTokenCount` and `Invocations` metrics at 1-minute granularity, plus the throttle count. The Service Quotas dashboard only shows configured limits, not live usage.
- If peak usage is roughly 1.5–2x your current TPM and only lasts a short time each day, request an increase and use cross-Region inference.
- If you're at the ceiling for many hours a day, or you need guaranteed latency and capacity, price out provisioned throughput.
